rationale: B wins by pruning, not by sounding prettier. Its refusal of "Can one good quarter win back investors holding Allbirds below its IPO price?" shows it understands that stock context belongs inside the turnaround-numbers story, while A spends a whole angle on "Fewer stores, fewer shoes...latest sign DTC brands are shrinking to survive" without evidence that this is a sector-wide trend. Both sets need real numbers and partner terms; B simply wastes less of the founder's time.
gaps_in_A: "latest sign DTC brands are shrinking to survive" turns one Allbirds update into a sector trend before the evidence is in. The proof section asks for comps, but the headline has already cashed the check.

"Allbirds swaps wool for a sugarcane blend it says will finally make its shoes last" overstates the product fact. The update says sugarcane-and-wool blend and company-claimed durability, not a wool swap or that prior shoes failed to last.
"brands are choosing fewer, better bets over growth-at-all-costs" imports a DTC morality play that is not in the supplied facts.
Angle 2 and angle 3 both lean on store closures as the strategic protagonist, so the set is a little padded even though the channel angle is real.
gaps_in_B: "store closures plus a 40% product-range cut producing the first quarter of gross-margin improvement" asserts causality the update does not give. That is the kind of tidy story reporters love to puncture.
"Allbirds' comeback runs through someone else's shelves" uses comeback language before the company has actually come back. It remains unprofitable; call it a relaunch or a turnaround bet.
"category-creation" is the wrong label for the sugarcane-and-wool angle. This is a materials/durability claim under scrutiny, not evidence that a category is being created.
The first angle names a retail/DTC trade reporter but underplays the capital-markets audience created by "publicly traded," "net-loss-making," and "well below its IPO price."
